awd_titl_txt: STTR Phase I:  Enhancing Career Decision-making for Individuals with ASD Through Adaptive Vocational Assessment Using Reinforcement Learning
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader/commercial impact of this Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) Phase I project lies in its transformative approach to addressing the critical employment challenges faced by over 5 million autistic adults in the U.S. where unemployment rates soar as high as 85% and many remain underemployed. Current vocational assessments are not only costly and time-consuming but also fail to capture the unique strengths of these individuals. This unique innovation leverages advanced reinforcement learning (RL) integrated with an immersive virtual reality (VR) environment to gather detailed skills, interests, and behavioral data, thereby enabling precise and adaptive job matching. This project enhances scientific and technological understanding by exploring the intersection of AI and VR within the field of neurodiversity, setting a new benchmark for personalized career support. Initially serving high school students and job training programs, the system is poised for expansion into state vocational rehabilitation agencies, creating a sustainable, subscription-based commercial model that provides a durable competitive advantage. By empowering autistic individuals to secure meaningful employment, the solution not only meets a significant market need but also promises to measurably reduce economic dependency projected to reach $11.5 trillion by 2029 to enhance workplace success to positively impact thousands of lives by year three.

This Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) Phase I project addresses the critical challenge of vocational assessment for individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) by developing an innovative AI-powered virtual reality (VR) system. The project aims to overcome the limitations of conventional evaluation methods by integrating advanced cognitive modeling and reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms to deliver adaptive, personalized vocational assessments and job matching solutions. The research involves simulating real-world vocational environments within VR to capture comprehensive performance metrics and behavioral data. In parallel, synthetic data generation via cognitive models replicates ASD-specific interaction patterns, thereby augmenting the training dataset for the RL framework. This dual approach enables continuous optimization of assessment strategies and job recommendation algorithms based on real-time user feedback. The anticipated technical results include improved accuracy in skill assessment and job matching, reduced evaluation bias, and enhanced predictive performance of vocational outcomes. Moreover, the system’s design incorporates a scalable framework amenable to integration into existing vocational training and human resources infrastructures, thereby offering substantial commercial potential. By leveraging interdisciplinary principles from AI, human-computer interaction, and behavioral sciences, this project promises significant advancements in personalized vocational evaluation and employment integration.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This NSF Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) Phase I project explored novel and innovative ways to help autistic individuals identify career paths that align with their strengths, interests, and abilities. Many autistic adults experience unemployment or underemployment despite possessing valuable skills and talents. Existing vocational assessments often rely on subjective observations, self-report measures, or limited opportunities to demonstrate real-world abilities. The goal of this project was to investigate whether virtual reality and artificial intelligence could provide an approach to vocational assessment and career planning that is more objective, engaging, and accessible than anything currently available.

During Phase I, the project team accomplished all goals set for the project by successfully developing and testing a virtual reality vocational assessment prototype that allows users to complete workplace activities in an immersive office environment. The system was designed to collect objective information about how individuals perform vocational tasks, including measures related to accuracy, work pace, and task engagement. The research included usability testing with autistic and non-autistic adolescents and young adults to evaluate accessibility, engagement, and user experience. Participants successfully completed all assessment activities, reported high levels of engagement, and described the virtual environment as realistic and meaningful. Overall, this study demonstrated that virtual reality can serve as a feasible and effective platform for capturing objective performance data relevant to vocational assessment.

Perhaps the most important outcome of the project was a significant research finding that changed the future direction of development. The original concept explored the use of artificial intelligence to generate vocational recommendations based on user performance data. Through development and testing, the research team identified important challenges related to scalability, data requirements, and the ability to clearly explain how recommendations were generated. The research revealed that transparency is especially important when developing technologies that may influence educational and career decisions for individuals with disabilities.

Career recommendations can shape how individuals view their own abilities and future opportunities. For autistic individuals, there is a risk that recommendations generated by a black box system could be interpreted as prescriptive rather than informative. A user may incorrectly conclude that a recommended occupation represents the only career path for which they are suited, potentially limiting exploration of other opportunities. As a result, the project demonstrated that vocational assessment technologies must provide recommendations that are transparent, explainable, and auditable by users, families, educators, and vocational professionals. 

The broader impacts of this work extend beyond the immediate project. The findings contribute to scientific understanding of how virtual reality and artificial intelligence can be responsibly applied in education, workforce development, and disability services.The ability to understand why a recommendation was made is not only a technical requirement but also an ethical safeguard that supports informed decision-making, personal autonomy, and self-determination when technology is used to support career planning and employment decisions. By identifying the need for transparent and explainable recommendations, the project contributes to the growing field of responsible artificial intelligence and may help guide the future development of assessment technologies serving autistic individuals and other underserved populations.This finding represents a major outcome of the research and provides a clearer path forward for developing technology that can be trusted, understood, and responsibly implemented in real-world settings.

The project also highlighted the importance of designing assessment tools that are accessible to individuals with a wide range of sensory, motor, and communication needs. These findings establish a stronger scientific foundation for future research aimed at creating scalable, accessible, and evidence-based assessment tools that can be used in schools, workforce programs, vocational rehabilitation services, and other settings. Ultimately, this work has the potential to expand access to high-quality vocational assessment, improve career planning, and support more meaningful employment opportunities for autistic individuals and other underserved populations. 

Products resulting from this project include a functional virtual reality vocational assessment prototype, software tools supporting performance measurement and analysis, usability and feasibility data, and research findings related to technology-assisted vocational assessment. These outcomes provide a foundation for future research and development aimed at improving employment outcomes through objective, accessible, and user-centered career assessment technologies.
